A Brief Discernment of the Nine Grades of the Method for Preparing Invitations, Shown to the Layman Xia Ziyi; An Invitation Shown to the Layman Ding Gengye;
An Invitation to the Layman Gu Zhaozheng; A Reply to the Layman Gu Zhaozheng.
The Discourse on the Names Given to the Layman Jinshuiuo; the Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Śūraṅgama by Avalokiteśvara;
the Three Characters Discourse on the Method for Contemplating the Buddha’s Ūrṇā-kośa;
and the Admonitions on the Pure Land.
The practice of the Bodhisattva Bhikṣu, exerting diligence to sever the floods and encouraging the arousal of true faith through the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation,
has a long history. Since our distant ancestor rose at Mount Lu and first established the Lotus Society, six...

Thus, the practice of Pure Conduct has established a fragrant standard for all ages. Although its daily merit is great and easy to advance in, practitioners in this degenerate age rarely obtain spiritual efficacy.
This is truly because their faith and aspiration are not single-minded, and they have been unable to guide their virtuous conduct toward the essential goal of rebirth in the Pure Land.
Now that you have widely invited virtuous companions to together cultivate the causes of purity, if you do not carefully examine and resolve to generate the bodhicitta, how can [this be achieved]?
One must know the essential path for escaping suffering. All you fellow beings who have gathered here for this Dharma assembly must possess genuine faith.

If one lacks true faith, then even though one recites the Buddha’s name, observes the fasts, releases living beings, and cultivates merit, these are merely the deeds of a worldly good person who is reborn in a favorable place to experience pleasure.
At the very moment of experiencing that pleasure, one begins to create karma; once karma has been created, one will inevitably fall back into suffering. This is the reality.
Observe this with your own eyes: compared to those icchantikas and candālas, we differ by only a single degree.
How could such faith be considered genuine? What is called "true faith" requires, first and foremost, the conviction that there is no difference between the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings.
I am a Buddha who has not yet realized it; Amitābha is a Buddha who has already realized it. Our enlightened nature (*bodhicitta*) is non-dual.
Although I am deluded and confused, the nature of my awakening has never been lost. Although I have transmigrated through kalpas, the nature of my awakening has never moved.
Therefore it is said: "Do not despise those who have not yet awakened; with a single thought of turning the light back upon itself, one is identical to what was originally attained.

Second, you must believe that I am the Buddha of the Principle-nature (li-xing) and the Buddha of Names (ming-zi), while Amitābha is the ultimate Buddha-nature. Although there are no two distinct positions, they are thus.

This is as vast as the difference between heaven and earth. If one does not single-mindedly recollect that Buddha and seek rebirth in that land, one will inevitably undergo the cycle of transmigration according to one's karma and suffer immeasurable pain;
this is what is meant by the Dharma-body transmigrating through the five realms, no longer called a Buddha, but termed a sentient being.
I believe with secondary conviction: though my hindrances are deep and my karma heavy, and I have long dwelt within the realm of suffering, I am a sentient being within the heart of Amitābha;
though Amitābha is adorned with myriad virtues and resides far beyond ten million billion lands, he is the Buddha within my own heart.
Since the nature of mind is non-dual, we naturally respond to one another through the convergence of the Way; thus, my bitter distress will surely—
It can indeed be evoked. The Buddha’s compassion will surely respond, just as a magnet attracts iron; there is no room for doubt. As it is said:
"The Buddha thinks of sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. If the child remembers the mother, just as the mother remembers the child, they shall be together throughout successive lives."
They are not at variance or distant from one another. If sentient beings mindfully recollect the Buddha with their hearts, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present or in the future;
they are not far from the Buddha. For those who possess the true faith described above, even a single hair’s breadth of goodness or a speck of dust’s worth of merit [will lead them there].

All of these may be dedicated toward the Western Land to adorn the Pure Land; how much more so for those who observe the fasts and uphold the precepts, release living beings, practice giving, recite the Mahāyāna sūtras, make offerings to the Triple Gem, and perform various other virtuous deeds—how could these not suffice as provisions for the Pure Land?

It is simply because one's place of faith is not true that one consequently sinks into the outflows (*āsrava*). Therefore, in the current practice of cultivation, there is no other essential technique;

it is merely a matter of adding these three kinds of true faith during the twelve periods of the day and night. Then, regarding all conduct and practice, there will be no need for the trouble of changing one's course.
If you wish to abandon this gateway of deliverance and seek some other "primordial and subtle" method of work, then the masters of the various quarters would [behold you as follows]:
The forest groves and the boundary poles stand facing one another; it is sufficient to seek the ford at any point along the way, without needing to set foot within this very community.

If your resolve is truly such that the deluded mind is forever extinguished and your pure aspirations are identical to mine, then may we fortunately assemble whenever the time and conditions are right.

With the faint sound of the lotus-water clock and the gentle jingle of the sedan chair, let it be so from ancient times to the present, and may this lingering tradition not fade away. May it serve as a bridge for us to become close companions in future lives.
May this very world serve as the necessary equipment for mutual inspiration; I pray that we shall both exert ourselves together.

To offer further exhortation, I cite the words of the former Master Zhenxie: "Buddha after Buddha hands it over; Patriarch after Patriarch transmits it to one another. It is solely this one matter; there is nothing else."
Regarding other matters: Śākyamuni Buddha dwelt in this world for seventy-nine years and preached the Dharma in over three hundred assemblies.

Yet, he alone spoke with persistent and earnest praise regarding the teaching of the Pure Land, never ceasing. Is it not because he regarded this as the swift path for transcending the mundane and entering the state of sagehood?
Nevertheless, this Dharma gate is both truly easy and truly difficult. For while one may uphold the Name and cultivate various merits...

Excellent. By sincerely dedicating [your merit], you will immediately attain rebirth there. If you indeed attain rebirth, you will cross the five paths of existence horizontally and transcend the three realms of existence instantly.
You will directly ascend to the stage of non-retrogression without passing through many *kalpas*. Is this not simple and easy? However, as for the worldly affairs of this Sahā world...

These concerns constantly entangle the mind; one day of cultivation followed by ten days of neglect means the heart lacks single-minded devotion. When encountering the five desires, one becomes as sticky as glue or lacquer;

when meeting adverse conditions, one harbors resentment and bitterness. Yet, at the moment of death, the Buddha’s welcoming guidance is a possibility that can hardly be expected—how difficult this is!
Viewed from this perspective, the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is like medicine for the greed of this Sahā world.

Affection is a taboo. Sentient beings suffer from the disease of karma; they are taught to revere the King of Physicians (the Buddha). Once they have begun to take his medicine, would it be right for them to again satiate themselves with that which is forbidden?
When the time comes for their lives to end, they fall back into their habitual tendencies; their pure causes are weak, and it is difficult for them to escape the wheel of suffering.
To the contrary, you would be saying that the King of Physicians has misled people and that the Buddha-dharma lacks efficacy—how tragic! Such people have reached the height of delusion.

Why do you not consider that at the Dharma-society of Mount Lu, eighteen eminent worthies and one hundred and twenty-three others all left behind auspicious responses, which are fully recorded in historical annals?

From the sun and moon of antiquity to those of today, from the mountains and rivers of the past to those of the present, they were already great men; how could we not be so as well? You ought to reflect upon this.

To know otherwise is simply because one has failed to release the mind from its heavy attachments and allow it to descend. All you who are gathered here—monastics and laypeople, old and young alike—should each feel deep anguish and reflect upon the perilous evils of this Sahā world.

You must strive early to seek liberation. There is a difference as vast as that between heaven and abyss between the crawling existence of the six realms and the carefree wandering of the nine grades of rebirth;
you must awaken to this with great urgency. You must certainly give rise to a profound sense of joy for the pure and revulsion for the defiled, and abandon all that is foul.

Adopt purity. Believe that this process of adopting and rejecting, as well as non-adopting and non-rejecting, are fundamentally not divergent paths. Do not pursue empty fame; do not cling to nihilistic views;
do not accept the high-capped, superficial talk of Chan practitioners. Do not be deluded by the mere names of samādhi; do not seek immediate results in the short term.
Do not harbor vain hopes that a Buddha will come from outside to welcome you, for this stirs up various demonic activities.

Whether at home or when joining a community, always take the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha as the primary practice (*maula-pratipatti*) and the diligent cultivation of various virtues as the auxiliary practice (*sahakāri-pratipatti*).

Furthermore, apply deliberate effort to scrub away the habitual tendencies of greed and anger, so that what is heavy becomes light and what is raw gradually matures. Maintain pure mindfulness in succession, and thus fulfill your vows and practices.
By supporting one another, all will naturally become a thousandfold secure and a hundredfold appropriate. Among the various practices, the single act of releasing living beings is the most excellent.
One should simply reflect deeply upon this: although they belong to the same general category of sentient beings, they still belong to different species; yet we still feel the need to save them.

How much more so for those of our own kind, whose obstructions are deep and whose karma is heavy—some of whom will before long fall into the evil realms, and some of whom are already on the brink of such a fate in this very life.
As for those suffering in hell, the agony of that place is more intense than the swords and fires of this world by no less than a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand times.
How can one allow such beings to be cast aside as if they were mere skin and membranes, failing to devise means for their salvation? Yet the method for their salvation lies solely in this very day:

to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name to be swiftly reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), and thereafter, riding upon the wheel of the Original Vow, to transport [them] with great...
By means of supernormal powers, you manifest unconditioned compassion and expand upon coessential pity.

You emanate bodies and project shadows throughout the lands of the ten directions and within all evil realms, seeking out voices to rescue those from suffering, just like Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; you vow to empty the hells, just like Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva;
and you uproot the causes and effects of suffering for all sentient beings, bestowing upon them both mundane and supramundane [benefits].

To rejoice in gathering all sentient beings so that they may together behold their compassionate father Amitābha and reach the state of ultimate peace—only one who possesses such a vow is a true man of integrity.
If one does not possess such a vow, then at the appointed time, we shall merely gather as a group.

To engage in these activities with such lingering indifference—though one may recite the Buddha’s name and practice the release of living beings—is nothing more than ordinary social convention. How could this be said to lack merit?
It is certainly not what I, a humble monk, hope for from my esteemed virtuous friends. I pray that you will examine and choose carefully.

Furthermore, I shall again urge [you] toward the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land. Although it is praised by all Buddhas and patriarchs alike, the men and gentlemen of this age have never before set eyes upon the teachings of a single lifetime.
Were it not for having possessed spiritual roots from past lives, how could one hear of it and believe with deep conviction? Now, for...

I shall briefly cite one or two essential treatises from the great sūtras to represent the rest, so that you may know the extraordinary excellence of these Dharma-gates and easily give rise to a mind of faith and joy.
Take, for example, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* alone: its teaching is vast and expansive, serving as the king among all sūtras.
It is like the bright sun in the sky, which eclipses the luster of the myriad stars; or like Mount Sumeru spanning the sea, which surpasses the height of all other peaks. Its...
This refers to the world-system. It is not said to be "as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," but rather "as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields.

Through the power of his wisdom and spiritual penetrations, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva surveys with a single eye the boundless seas of fragrant water and the boundless lands, as clearly as a fruit in the palm of his hand.
From the near to the far, according to each respective direction, he points them out one by one.
The names, titles, and characteristics are as follows: the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) is situated within the fundamental realm of Vairocana.

This realm consists of twenty tiers, being broad at the top and narrow at the bottom, shaped like an inverted pagoda. Both the Sahā world and the World of Ultimate Bliss reside on the thirteenth tier.
Within this tier, there are worlds surrounding it as numerous as the atoms in thirteen Buddha-fields. [The World of] Ultimate Bliss...

The world is but a single number. When compared to the multitude of worlds in the original land, it is like taking all the grain harvested over a hundred years throughout the entire continent of Jambudvīpa and making it into a single heap; the world would be comparable to a single grain of millet therein.
How much more so when considering all the worlds within the boundless clusters of lands beyond the original land—how could they even be described, conceived, or calculated? Thus it is.

At the conclusion of this vast scripture, one is led back to the Land of Ultimate Bliss by means of the Ten Great Vows, solely to ensure rebirth in the World of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) and to enable the vision of Amitābha Buddha.

This earnest exhortation and repeated, emphatic instruction are fully contained within the "Chapter on Practice and Vows" (Pranidhāna-paṭala); they shall not be recorded here at length. Furthermore, six hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa...
The Twelfth Patriarch of the Western Heaven, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa, in accordance with the Buddha’s prophetic decree, restored the True Dharma.

Taking one hundred lakṣas of Mahāyāna sūtras as his foundation, he composed a single treatise titled *Awakening of Faith*. This work enables sentient beings of the final age to give rise to the correct faith of the Mahāyāna;
it is like weaving together various colors to form brocade, or distilling a hundred flowers to produce perfume.
Honey. His expositions and analyses of principle exhaust the subtle and reach the ultimate.

Having fully set forth all the various dharma-gates and samādhis to cause [practitioners] to cultivate right faith, he further reflects that all these various dharma-gates and samādhis are difficult to practice and easy to regress from.
Thus, at the very end, he again reveals the superior and extraordinary skillful means of all Buddhas, saying: "Furthermore, for the beginner..."
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this Sahā world, they may encounter the sufferings of untimely cold, heat, wind, rain, or famine;
or they may see sentient beings who are unwholesome and fearsome, entangled by the three poisons and habitually practicing evil dharmas. Yet, the Bodhisattva remains amidst them.

If one’s mind becomes timid and weak, fearing that pure faith cannot be accomplished, and if doubt arises such that one wishes to retreat, one should make a vow to single-mindedly and exclusively recollect the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas.
Because of the arising of this resolute mind, at the end of life in this world, [one will be reborn in the Pure Land].
One will certainly attain rebirth within the buddha-fields of the various Buddhas, behold the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and forever leave the evil realms behind. As it is said in the sutras:

"If good sons and good daughters single-mindedly keep Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss in mind and dedicate all their roots of goodness toward the vow for rebirth there, they will certainly attain rebirth. They will constantly see that Buddha, their faith will increase, and they will never again..."
One turns back from [the cycle of birth and death] and attains entry into the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

Thus we know that during the Buddha’s lifetime, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, and after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna—such great beings as these all exhorted [beings] to be born [in the Pure Land], while also vowing to go themselves to draw near to Amitābha.
Furthermore, in other major sūtras such as the *Ratnakūṭa* and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, the praises and exhortations are so numerous they cannot easily be cited in full. Nevertheless...

The pure lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions are immeasurable; yet, the reason why the sutras and śāstras specifically point toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) involves, in brief, three intentions.
First, because that Buddha has the deepest affinity with the people of this land: regardless of noble or humble status, wise or foolish, young or old, all know the name of Amitābha Buddha.
If they encounter suffering or distress, there is no one who, upon opening their mouth and raising their voice, does not invoke his name.

Regarding the name: because the power of the vows of the bhikṣu Dharmākara was supreme, he took the various adornments of twenty-one billion pure Buddha-lands and consolidated them into the single adornment of one land, the World of Ultimate Bliss.

He then made forty-eight great vows to extensively welcome sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha throughout the ten directions to be reborn in his land. Although the fruit-virtues of all Buddhas—though [vast]...
Reality is equal. Through the power of vows within the causal stage, beings are spontaneously gathered; thus, within non-differentiation there is differentiation.
Third, Amitābha Buddha is the very body of the Dharma-realm treasury, and the Land of Ultimate Bliss is the Lotus-treasury Ocean.
To see one Buddha is to see immeasurable Buddhas; to be born in one land is to be born in immeasurable lands; to contemplate one Buddha...
This is precisely to be mindful of all Buddhas, which constitutes being protected and remembered by all Buddhas.

This is because the Dharma-body is non-dual, because the Buddha and sentient beings are non-dual, and because the one who is mindful and that which is minded are non-dual. Although various sutras and treatises extensively praise this practice, among the sentient beings of this land, there were originally none who knew it.
It was only the Venerable Huiyuan of the Jin dynasty who rose at Mount Kuanglu and first established the Lotus Samādhi.
At that time, famous worthies and great scholars arrived spontaneously without prior invitation; figures such as Liu Yimin and Zong Lei all took up the teachings with devotion and sought instruction.
Consequently, the Way flourished greatly. Since the Tang and Song dynasties, Chan studies have gradually become widespread.

Among the scholar-officials, those possessed of wisdom and discernment have for the most part held a refined admiration for the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), their aspirations being lofty and extraordinary. Yet, throughout the span of over a thousand years, from top to bottom...
In recent times, those who were truly able to see their nature have been no more than a few individuals, such as Minister Yang Yi, Prince Consort Li Zunxu, and Langzhong Xu Shi;
all others were merely those who dabbled at the gateway of the teachings.
Consequently, this inconceivable and extraordinary Dharma-gate has been left in the hands of commoners and women. Although there were three or five venerable masters in the interim...

Successive generations have transmitted these teachings from master to disciple; yet, it was not necessarily the case that they frequently encountered eminent practitioners or extensively saved the masses.

It was toward the end of the Ming dynasty that the Great Master Yunqi Hongwu appeared, inheriting the compassionate vows of his predecessors. Having emerged from the mundane world as a refined scholar, he specialized in propagating the Pure Land practice.
While there were many renowned worthies of the age who took refuge in his faith, those who harbored doubts, offered criticisms, or raised challenges were likewise numerous. Great...

With his vast talent and wondrous eloquence, the Master remained unbowed through a hundred battles, instead transforming them into the joy of Dharma-pleasure (*dharmaprīti*). Consequently, both monastics and laypeople were delighted and submitted to him;
he was as if Huiyuan had been reborn, and Yongming had returned for a second life. Thus, the Way of the Pure Land once again attained great resurgence.
This truly revives a dharma gate that had fallen into decline for over a thousand years; how magnificent is its merit! Alas, it has now departed.
In the dark alleys of the Dharma-ending age, when sentient beings are heavily defiled, we have lost this excellent guide amidst the perilous and evil paths—how can one not sigh deeply at this?
Born too late, I was unable to personally attend upon the Great Master; I shall instead treasure his legacy.
I said: "How could it be merely like jade or ceremonial vessels? Every time I unroll and read his writings, I cannot help but have tears flow down my cheeks; my heart and mind are stirred with vigor.

Since I have resided here at Puren, I have constantly had the privilege of gathering with a multitude of worthies, practicing the Way during the six periods of the day, which fully accords with my long-held aspirations.
Yet, whenever I encounter a companion for a meeting, I do not dare regard them as a mere worldly man; in my private heart, I secretly [regard them as such]."
He calculated and said: "Within the land of Lotus, there shall be yet another eminent companion.
Long ago, our original teacher Śākyamuni made a prophetic declaration that sixty-seven billion bodhisattvas from this land would be reborn in that country; this must surely be one such number.

Although I know that many will eventually fall away over time, once they have resolved their minds to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, they have already entered the ocean of Amitābha’s vows. Just so...
If a person consumes even a small amount of vajra, it will never be digested. Regardless of whether one is diligent or indolent, slow or fast, in the end, they will certainly be born in that land.
Once born in that land, they will ultimately attain the realization of the fruit and achieve the Way through the eight phases, extensively delivering all sentient beings.
Therefore, when you have just entered this assembly, it is not a falsehood for me to expect you to become future Buddhas.
However, I do not know how you yourself regard yourselves as fellow practitioners.
If you can indeed regard yourselves as I have expected, then all the virtuous friends present before you will be like lotus buds sharing the same branch. Yet, as I observe the wealthy of today...

Those who seek noble status and prosperity may greedily crave coarse sounds and colors, failing to recognize the root of suffering; they may be attached to fame and reputation as small as a snail’s horn, failing to awaken to their illusory nature;
or they may love to accumulate wealth and profit, calculating and managing them until their entire present life passes in a state of mundane toil.

In the future, as they drift through the cycle of rebirth according to their karma, they will neither hear of nor know of the infinite, supreme, and wondrous joys of that Buddha-field, nor its adornments of the environment and its inhabitants.
From birth until death, they will never once give rise to a single thought of longing for it;

on the contrary, they will be no different from the destitute and the afflicted, who are often able to recite the Buddha’s name, thereby passing from darkness into light and being reborn in superior realms. Therefore...
I now respectfully exhort all my friends: since you have each inscribed your names in the Lotus Society, you are surely among those rare *udumbara* flowers within the burning house.
You must possess true aspirations, giving rise to a mind of joy in the transcendental and weariness with the mundane;

regarding the three realms as a prison, the home and garden as shackles, sounds and forms as lethal poison, fame and profit as fetters, and the vicissitudes of fortune and misfortune over several decades as...
It is like a dream from yesterday. Regard this single lifetime of retribution in the Sahā world as merely a brief stay in a guesthouse that must be left behind;
let your sole task be returning home. Whether you encounter what is favorable or unfavorable, cast aside every moment and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name.
If, by doing so, you are unable to be born in the Pure Land, then all the Buddhas would be speaking falsehoods. May we together—
Exert yourselves!

To those who wish to undertake a three-year long-term practice of nianfo (Buddha-recitation) so that their spiritual cultivation and practice shall not be in vain, you should give rise to three kinds of resolve as your method.
It is well. First, one must feel a profound sense of regret regarding the passage of time. Although the mind may resolve upon a period of three years, the time that passes is but brief.
As the ancients have likened it to a continuous malarial fever, where the chills and fevers recur three times; before long, the term will have come to an end.

Unless one diligently exerts both body and mind, competing with every fraction of a moment, one cannot avoid finding this duration too long. If one finds it too long, then over the course of idle years, there will be nothing gained.
Without a broad and open mind, weariness easily arises and pure merit cannot be achieved; is this not deeply regrettable? Moreover, life hangs by a thread; who can guarantee three years?
Even if one were to exceed three years, how could it last long? It is as the saying goes: "Like a prisoner heading to the marketplace."
It is like a sheep going to the slaughterhouse; it can only move forward, step by step drawing closer to death.

You must simply be diligent day and night, persevering through heat and cold, reciting the Great Name with no interval for rest. Without needing to be escorted by Amitābha to the Pure Land, you will certainly be reborn there.
All you fellow practitioners, be careful not to be sharp at the beginning but lax at the end; you should regard three years as a single day.

It takes but a single kṣaṇa. Second, one must develop the resolute intention to seek liberation. Now, these three years of practice and cultivation are not merely for the sake of seeking worldly blessings and rewards;
nor are they for the sake of seeking merit, wisdom, eloquence, or realization, nor for the aspiration to serve as a monk in life after life to cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish and manifest.
One’s sole wish is that, at the end of this life, one may attain birth in that land and be liberated.
The suffering of birth and death—this vow must manifest before you at every moment. It is like a man of old who was covered over and cast into a dry well a thousand feet deep;
he received the instruction of a wild fox to fix his gaze upon the hole and, with single-minded intent, desired to escape.

After gazing for a long time, the hole did not grow larger and his body did not grow smaller, yet he spontaneously flew out. Reciting the Buddha’s name is also like this: recite that Buddha exclusively with a single mind.
Seeking birth [in the Pure Land], their mindfulness becomes so earnest that, although the Buddha does not actually come and they do not actually go, they naturally attain rebirth.
Having fulfilled this one vow, they see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, sever delusions, and realize the fruit; without relying on expedient means, they spontaneously attain the opening of the mind.
Hundreds of thousands of samādhis manifest before them as soon as they are thought of, and unspeakably, unspeakably many great vows, as numerous as atoms, are simultaneously fulfilled.
It is essential to be fully endowed with sincere faith and diligent practice, focusing exclusively and single-mindedly; only then can one achieve success.

Third, develop a mind that is harmonious, compliant, and observant of restraint. Since there are not many people within the hall, you shall dwell together morning and evening as fellow practitioners and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Each of you should guard your conduct and protect your speech, remaining humble, respectful, and yielding. You should encourage one another and serve as mutual models for one another. This...
Within three years—for example, during a period of seclusion and retreat—one must take the mountain gate as the boundary and may not go outside.

Even in the event of a serious illness or death among close relatives or friends, one must not break this rule by going out. This would set a precedent for others to follow and provide an opening for self-indulgence.
One’s daily constant practices must not be neglected or omitted, except in cases of illness where it is physically impossible.
Whether eating or drinking, sitting or lying down, one must likewise silently recite the Buddha’s name. Indeed, within the state of illness, this is especially urgent.
Beyond one's regular daily recitations, if there is remaining time, one must examine oneself; do not let the body and mind pass in vain.
One must not engage in idle chatter, frivolous talk, or heedless laughter, which would lead to self-delusion and hinder others. Furthermore, one must not peruse secular books or recite poetry.

To recite verses and hymns is not merely to waste one's time; it is also to fail the donors (dānapati). One person shall be appointed from the main hall to serve as the *jianzhi* (supervisor on duty), with the term changing every five days.
A notice board shall be posted for the handover of duties. Should there be anyone who fails to observe the rules or act according to the Dharma, the *jianzhi* must offer counsel and admonition.
If the person listens after a single admonition, that is well. If they do not listen after three admonitions, the matter shall be reported to the assembly.

The penalties shall be deliberated upon. If the supervising masters or those on duty yield to personal bias and conceal faults, failing to offer admonition or report infractions, they shall be punished proportionally according to the specific matter.
However, if the various masters maintain strict self-discipline and each strives with diligence and heedfulness, such regulations may be set aside as superfluous.
This is most excellent. Exert yourselves! Exert yourselves!
On the occasion of the seven-day period for arousing *vīrya*, I address the assembly:

for these seven days, hold fast to the Name. The essential point lies in single-mindedness without distraction, being uninterrupted and unmixed; it does not necessarily depend on the rapidity or frequency of recitation.
Mindfulness is paramount. However, one should be neither lax nor hurried; maintain the name closely and steadily, so that the Buddha’s name is vividly clear within the mind.
Whether dressing or eating, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, let this single great name be continuous and uninterrupted, much like the act of breathing.
Since it is neither distracted nor sunken, such recitation of the name may be called "the practice of the phenomenal."

This is one who is able to practice with single-minded diligence. Being such a true member of the lineage of the Way, they are able to directly investigate all phenomena (*dharmas*) as being entirely without dualistic characteristics.
That is to say: birth and Buddhahood are non-dual; self and other are non-dual; self and other are non-dual;

the environment and its inhabitants are non-dual; purity and defilement are non-dual; suffering and pleasure are non-dual; joy and aversion are non-dual; grasping and abandoning are non-dual; and Bodhi...
Afflictions and nirvana are non-dual; birth-and-death and nirvana are non-dual. All these dualistic dharmas share one and the same characteristic:

the single path of purity. There is no need for forced effort or contrived arrangement; simply investigate the reality of things as they are. When this investigation reaches its ultimate limit, there is a sudden, spontaneous accord with one’s own original mind.
