Regarding what are called difficult practices and ascetic austerities—things I have never performed before and am incapable of performing—I am filled with deep admiration.
They cannot be sufficiently praised through brush or tongue; reading this long poem truly accords with the man’s character. Reading it again and again, I find it ever more refined and beautiful.
In the past, Lu Zhiang was eighty when he still indulged in his verse, and Qiu Wei was ninety when he excelled at composing fu; as for the Layman, his age...

While residing between Qiū and Hè, you have engaged in literary composition, excelling in both arts. I hope that you will now cherish every moment of the passing shadows and grow indifferent to your fondness for brush and ink.
Redirect this vigor and apply your mind solely to pure practices; thus, the sprouts of wisdom will flourish.

Through the maturation of the seeds of the Path, one day you will be born by transformation upon a lotus flower before the Buddha; at that point, you will no longer be on the same level as those such as Qiu He.
This is the reply to Layman Gu Zhaozheng.

I previously sent you several lines by mail, which I trust you have already perused. Recently, I received your letter, in which you spoke of how worldly karmic attachments and emotional entanglements are difficult to dissolve, and asked when one might achieve "wondrous contemplation" (*pratyavekṣā*).
From these words, it is clear that your earnestness in seeking the Way is profound.

However, according to my humble view, this very state of wearying oneself with the dust of the world while longing for wondrous contemplation is precisely what constitutes the study of the Way. For now, one should avoid internal obstacles and seek out quietude.
In a place of stillness, before the world has yet produced its defilements, can the emotions truly be severed? One must understand that the myriad dharmas are fundamentally tranquil;
it is only man who creates his own clamor. Excellent indeed are the words of Master Ouyi:

"Though it is said that the six sense organs wander in illusion and the six emotions stir in confusion, if one investigates carefully, the objects do not bear the blame, nor do the organs themselves hold the fault. Since the organs—
If one does not fulfill their duty, how could their transgression be borne by others alone? When analyzed through the three categories (*trividha-paryeṣaṇā*), there is no true master;

even if they were combined, what substantial dharma (*bhūta-dharma*) could there be? Yet we, within these deceptive dharmas, cling to "self" and indulge in "person," rejecting that and grasping this—just like the chaotic flowers that appear when one rubs the eyes.
We further wish to discriminate the characteristics of these flowers, asking which is beautiful and which is not.
This is indeed ugly; is it not also erroneous? Only by letting go of the entirety of body, mind, and the world will the eye of wisdom become radiant and clear;

where then would there be any defiled emotions to loathe? However, if one wishes to practice *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, it is perfectly permissible to vigorously give rise to a mind of longing and aversion.
If this mind of longing and aversion is clung to, it becomes a delusive affliction; if it is fully understood, it is a skillful means.
It depends entirely upon the person. As for what is called "sublime contemplation," does the *Contemplation Sūtra* not say:

"The ocean of the Tathāgatas' correct and universal knowledge arises from the mind's thoughts. When sentient beings contemplate the Buddha with their minds, that very mind is the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
that mind creates the Buddha; that mind is the Buddha. These few words alone constitute the practice of nianfo (Buddha-recitation).

The secret essentials of samādhi and all gates of contemplation flow forth from this; for if one knows how to practice but does not know what is [the ultimate], one falls into the provisional and the Lesser Vehicle.
If one knows what is but does not know how to practice, one will surely fall into the ranks of Māras and externalists. Practice is the contemplations of emptiness and provisionality;
"what is" is the contemplation of the Middle Way. When "what is" is entirely practice and practice is entirely "what is," this is the three contemplations within a single thought-moment.

Because they are perfectly interfused, a verse from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says: "If one enters [meditation] by merely recollecting Amitābha Buddha, this is called the unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous dhyāna.
When one perceives the Buddha through visualization with focused thought, that is itself the Dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Master Zhijue said: "In a single thought-moment of resonance, there is a Buddha; in every thought-moment of resonance, there is a Buddha. The Buddha is original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*)."

This is the principle: namely, the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-jñāna*). Therefore, one should know that at the very moment of correct mindfulness of the Buddha, the initial and the fundamental merge;

wisdom and principle are in profound resonance; subject and object are both forgotten; self and other are non-dual; there is no Buddha outside of mindfulness to be the object of recollection, and no mindfulness outside of the Buddha that can recollect the Buddha.
Transcending emotion and views, free from words and beyond negation, it is direct, immediate, perfect, and sudden. There is none...
Beyond this, apart from the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti), what other sublime contemplation could possibly be accomplished?

I have reflected on this privately: medicine has no inherent nobility or baseness; that which cures the illness is what is efficacious. Whether one treats the root or the symptoms, one should act according to the urgency of the situation.

You, Layman, are at an age of advanced years; though you have turned your mind toward the Way, even if you were to live a hundred years, how much of that remaining light would there be? Should you not consider restraining [your senses] and [focusing your efforts]?
While one exerts effort on a path that is most stable and easy, does one still seem to be probing for the profound mystery?
Does one linger and gaze longingly between them? When we met previously, I did not merely refrain from discussing "wondrous contemplation" (*myōkan*);
I even dispensed with many types of daily recitations, urging you instead to rely solely upon the six-syllable mantra. This is a marvelous remedy from the sea, capable of treating urgent ailments.

Regarding illness, moreover, one should treat both the root and the symptoms simultaneously, ensuring that the response is appropriate to the urgency of the situation. What is most important is deep faith and diligent practice.
As the ancients said: "If one sees only Amitābha, why worry about not attaining enlightenment? Thus, what worldly passions would not be dissolved and extinguished?
What samādhi would not manifest before you? Yet today, even if there were hundreds of thousands of dharma-gates and immeasurable subtle meanings, set them all aside and do not employ them;
I offer you only this single-flavored, simple remedy. If one does not apply oneself with total concentration—cutting through like a chisel striking iron—how can one extricate oneself?
If you insist that the efficacy of holding the name is inferior to other methods...
As for visualization, the physical marks and features possessed by that Buddha are subtle and wondrous, and the contemplative methods revealed in the sutras and treatises are profound and intricate;
those at the initial stage of the ordinary world may find it difficult to accomplish. Ultimately, it is more stable and reliable to rely on the shorter sutra and single-mindedly hold the Name.

However, when holding the Name, if one thoroughly understands both the phenomenal and the noumenal aspects with a mind that is not distracted, this itself constitutes the object of visualization; there is no need for [further effort].
Do not seek elsewhere. Layman Nian Yuanmiao is one of profound sincerity; disregarding the vast difference in our ages, he has earnestly inquired of me.
Therefore, I venture to set forth my humble and straightforward thoughts without any concealment or hesitation. I pray only that you will examine them and choose from them as you see fit.

Regarding the explanation of the "name" (mingzi) stage, Master Jinshui Ruojushi of Tiantai distinguished it from other stages using the six Buddhas. The first is called the "principle-nature" (lixing), and the second is called the "name" (mingzi).

From the initial hearing of the sacred teachings up until the clarification of the mind and realization of the nature, one has not yet emerged from the position of the name; thus, we know that the duration of this stage of the name is extremely long. However...
The meaning of this is likewise profound and immeasurable. A householder was named Shan (Good) and styled Shui Ruo (Water-like).

To understand this name and recognize this style is to have completed more than half the work on the path of attaining Buddhahood through seeing one's nature. He told his son: "Nature is like a rushing torrent."
If one diverts the flow toward the east, it flows east; if one diverts it toward the west, it flows west.
That human nature is not divided into good and evil is just as water is not divided between east and west. How extraordinary!
Gaozi’s discourse on human nature, though it does not represent the ultimate meaning of the Confucian tradition, nevertheless bears a resemblance to the sūtras of the Tathāgata. What a pity.
That he was defeated by Mencius’s arguments and ultimately unable to clarify his own doctrine is like an insect trying to ward off a mushroom.
For if the ten dharma realms are fundamentally rooted in the one mind, then it is clear that both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are inherently possessed within that nature.
What is meant is that within the nature (prakṛti) there exist seeds of both defilement and purity.

Therefore, among all phenomena, mundane or supramundane, not a single one exists that lies outside of this nature. To follow the pure seeds within the nature and give rise to their actualization is the way of the noble person;
it is called "cultivating goodness. To follow the defiled seeds within the nature and give rise to their actualization is the way of the petty person; it is called...
Regarding the cultivation of evil, the *Zhongyong* states: "To follow one's nature is called the Way. Confucius said: "The Way is twofold:
benevolence (*ren*) and non-benevolence (*bu-ren*) alone. If the Way were not divided into benevolence and non-benevolence, then nature would likewise not be divided into good and evil.
If nature were exclusively good and devoid of evil, then the three miserable realms and the evil destinies would not be created by the mind; furthermore, how could they be so designated?
Is it not the dharma-realm? Therefore, although an icchantika may sever cultivated goodness, they do not sever innate goodness.
If they were to sever innate goodness, they would ultimately never attain Buddhahood. The Buddhas and sages only sever cultivated evil; they do not sever innate evil.
If they were to sever innate evil, they would be unable to manifest in defiled and evil worlds to subdue sentient beings. This is the crux between the innate and the cultivated.
That which must be thoroughly penetrated is this: one cannot give rise to cultivation apart from nature, nor can one speak of nature while neglecting cultivation.
Let us take water as an illustration. What is called "nature" is its moisture and its tendency to flow downward, whether flowing east or west.
What is called "cultivation" is the act of diverting it toward the east or diverting it toward the west. If you, Layman, wish to practice cultivation...
Regarding the purification of karma, can one not examine the methods by which it is cultivated, rather than merely looking at the name? If one's mind, moment after moment,
inclines toward greed, hatred, and delusion— growing deeper and more severe day by day and month by month— such that pulling it back is impossible and leading it out is futile,
and its manifestations through body and speech are mostly associated with evil, then what is called "deciding for the East" will ultimately result in the land of Zhendan (China).
Among these people, if their minds are filled with a constant sense of weary detachment from the five desires, and they fix their thoughts upon Amitābha Buddha,
aspiring to draw near to him as a child remembers its mother, they will not be dragged away by the objects of karma nor deluded by divergent paths.

Thus, what is called "resolving toward the West" means to settle upon rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), to be born through transformation from a lotus flower, and to behold the Buddha and receive a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Viewed in this light, realizing Buddhahood by seeing one's nature also depends solely on such resolution.
If one can resolve toward the West so that one’s current flows westward, then one will certainly not enter the boiling waters of the three miserable realms (*trāya*), and certainly not...
It blends with the water of craving of humans and devas, yet does not mix with the turbid water of ordinary beings;
it is not stained by the foul water of Māras and externalists, nor does it fall into the death-water of the two vehicles.

It is not the same as the guest-water of the provisional vehicles, but constantly attains the water of principle to moisten the field of the mind, and the water of wisdom to harmonize the myriad practices. Thus, even within this stage of names and words, one is perfectly united with the Tathāgata.

Its nature is water. Once it has attained union with this natural water, it returns to the pool of the seven treasures, becoming clear and pure, cool and refreshing, sweet and delicious, light and soft, moist and lustrous, peaceful and harmonious, a remover of afflictions, and a source of increase.
Thus, it ultimately becomes the holy water endowed with the eight merits. Flowing westward, it reaches its limit here; truly, this is one who has fully realized the nature of water.
Furthermore, I have carefully examined the meaning of your layman’s name and style; they derive from the principles of Mencius.
This is not the doctrine of Gaozi. As for the definitive discernment of wholesome dharmas and their cultivation to fulfillment,

and the definitive destruction of unwholesome dharmas and their cultivation for elimination until they are exhausted— thereby causing the Way of the gentleman to flourish and the Way of the petty person to wane, and ultimately coming to rest in the ground of ultimate goodness—
this is never at variance with Gaozi, it is never at variance with Confucius, and it is likewise never at variance with [the Buddha].
This is in accord with the Great Sage of the Western Land. Layman, will you not exert your strength to resolve this?

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, specifically the chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Śrī Avalokiteśvara, is said to follow after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*; it is truly the inner sanctum of the Buddha-dharma. Formerly, the Master Zhiyi...

At the time of the classification of the teachings (panjiao), this sutra had not yet reached China; therefore, only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* were regarded as the "final flavor" (tī-mo).
Had they been able to see it at once, there would surely have been extensive commentaries and exegeses, and its inclusion within the *Amṛta* (Ghee) stage would have been beyond doubt.

Alas, since the Great Beings who are the Four Reliances (*catur-apāśraya*) have already passed away, the commentators of past and present have each promoted divergent views. For a long time, these disputes have been as voluminous as a public lawsuit, leaving later students lacking the means to discern the truth.

Regarding the Dharma-eye, there is nowhere to turn for guidance. To advocate that commentaries and exegeses be entirely discarded in favor of looking only at the scriptural text is itself an overly extreme argument.
Furthermore, when one attempts to seek the meaning of the scriptures through one's own intellect, one often fails to penetrate their essential intent, resulting ultimately in nothing but obscurity.
Let us examine this with an impartial mind: how could the various interpretations be devoid of merit? Yet, they do not fall into the error of contradiction.

This is erroneous; it is immediately lost in its oversimplification. Even among those whose insight is transcendent and who rise above their peers, they again rely on this sutra to expound what is within their own minds.

While their original treatises may possess truth, and they may be able to set aside their own views to follow the sutra and comply with the Buddha’s intent, I have seen nothing that can rival the excellence of Master Jia Yi’s *Shu* (Commentary) on the West Lake, with the exception of that single work. Who would say that people of the present day must necessarily...?

Can one not surpass the ancients? Some may find his advocacy excessive, and it is not without reason that they criticize him for fabricating [theories]. Even if there are indeed some regrets, he has nonetheless rendered great service to this scripture.

As for the teaching that abandons consciousness (*vijñāna*) to employ the sense organs (*indriya*), placing primary emphasis on the doctrine of perfect penetration—this is the sincere word of the Buddhas;

who would dare not believe it? Regarding the essence of the teachings in this land... [Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* (likely by Zongmi). The final sentence is incomplete.]
I dare not fail to comply with this. Those who debate against it are all those who contravene the scriptures and oppose the Buddha.
It is truly not easy to find those present here who have already set their minds upon the Pure Land and further wish to study this sutra.

Nevertheless, setting aside its beginning and end for a moment, there are many points of confusion and error within this very section on "Perfect Penetration" (Yuántōng). Unless one is skilled at reading and interpreting it, then—
It is said that the finest cream (*sarpis*) and poison are not far apart.
Have you not heard how, at the assembly of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*—the field where Buddhas are selected—Avalokiteśvara "passed the examination" while Mahāsthāmaprāpta "failed"?

For those who cultivate the Pure Land, if they do not discern this distinction here, how can they realize the esoteric intent of this sutra and strengthen the practice and vows of future students? It is simply a matter of the gateway of Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

Because this is not the essential meaning of this sutra, Master Jian also cited it in his commentary without further elaboration. Now, I shall first distinguish the dharma-gate and subsequently clarify its esoteric intent.
Regarding the distinction of the dharma-gate:
one should know that this holy, perfect penetration belongs to the seven elements (*dhātu*). Among these, the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*) universally encompasses the other six.

Because it is based on the faculties (*indriya*), one cultivates the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha by relying on these six faculties. There are three different types: first, mindfulness of one's own Buddha;
second, mindfulness of another Buddha; and third, mindfulness of both one's own and another Buddha. If one is mindful of one's own Buddha, this accords with the perfect penetration of all the Sages.
This is because the faculty-nature is taken as the dharma-gate that is the object of mindfulness, and the revolving of the profound stillness is taken as the means of mindfulness.
It is appropriate. As stated in the *Ugra-paripṛcchā Sūtra*: "That is to say, those eye-faculties of the Tathāgatas are always fully perfected and without diminution in their cultivation;
they see with perfect clarity and distinctness. ... And so on, up to: those mind-faculties of the Tathāgatas are always fully perfected and without diminution in their cultivation;
they know with perfect clarity and distinctness," and so forth. It is also like this sūtra, wherein the Buddhas of the ten directions collectively address Ānanda, commanding him...
"You shall swiftly realize the blissful liberation of wondrous, eternal quiescence. These are none other than your own six sense faculties.
As the Patriarch said: 'In the womb it is called the body; in the world it is called a person; in the eye it is called seeing; in the ear it is called hearing.'"
Discerning fragrance with the nose, engaging in discourse with the mouth, grasping with the hands, and running about with the feet—the one who recognizes these as the Buddha-nature calls them such;
the one who does not recognize them calls them the "vital spirit" (*jīng-hún*). The various patriarchs of antiquity have provided many such indications.
This mindfulness itself encompasses all doctrinal meanings within the Buddha’s samādhi and constitutes the direct pointing method-gate of all Chan schools, leaving nothing unexhausted.

It is not exhaustive. If one contemplates another Buddha, there is a difference from the perfect penetration of the various sages. One takes the six sense faculties as the subject of contemplation and the resultant Buddha as the object of contemplation.
Although the Dharma-body is indeed of one essence, I lack the two kinds of adornment, whereas the Buddhas have perfected merit and wisdom to become the Honored Ones with Two Feet.
Contemplating those resultant virtues, one does not give rise to weariness; the eyes constantly gaze [upon them].
The marks of the Buddha: the ears constantly hear the Buddha’s teachings; the nose constantly perceives the Buddha’s fragrance; the tongue constantly recites the Buddha’s name;

the body constantly prostrates before the Buddha’s image; and the mind constantly takes the Buddha’s Dharma as its object. That which is focused by the six sense faculties is nothing other than the realm of the Buddha.
Thus, these states succeed one another without interruption or confusion. This samādhi of mindfulness of another Buddha fully encompasses all [the practices of] Amitābha, Bhaiṣajyaguru, and Maitreya.
The *Sūtra on Birth* and other such texts, as well as the methods for contemplating all karmic actions and phenomena of the Lotus Society, are fully and exhaustively contained herein.

If one contemplates the Buddhas within oneself and others, one will achieve perfect penetration with all the sages; yet while being identical, there is still a distinction. First, one must open up a sudden and perfect understanding.

To thoroughly realize that the birth of a Buddha and one’s own mind are of one essence, and that the land and the mind are non-dual; to rely upon that environment and its inhabitants to manifest one's own mind-nature;

and thus, being no longer deluded regarding anything outside of this nature, neither to regard the existence of a Buddha as something external, nor to grasp at that land as being other than mind—this is the point where one opens the perfect understanding shared with all the sages.

To rely upon the objective realm of others is what distinguishes one from the sages. This is what the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations) refers to as the "superior and extraordinary skillful means."
The present text states that one need not rely on expedient means, for the mind opens of itself; because this expedient is most supreme and extraordinary, no further expedients are required.

Within the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuantun jiao*), we shall briefly distinguish the great function of gathering in sentient beings by correlating the three types of Buddha-remembrance samādhis (*nianfo sanmei*) with the four kinds of pure lands.
As for those who contemplate only their own Buddha, they are gathered back into the serene land of true recompense (*shibao*).

The light [of Avalokiteśvara] purifies two kinds of pure lands; however, it can only allow for vertical entry and cannot enable horizontal transcendence. Furthermore, it only accommodates those of sharp faculties and cannot universally embrace all.

Moreover, as this is common to all the sages, it does not manifest the unique distinction of this specific gate. Thus, it seems that this is not the essential intent of Śrī-Prabhāsa’s inclusion [of the practitioner].

Now, I maintain that it correctly encompasses two types of practitioners: those who practice mindfulness of another Buddha and those who practice mindfulness of both self and other Buddhas. It leads them back...
Within the Land of Common Abode, one simultaneously and transversely transcends the lands of Expedient Means, True Reward, and Peaceful Light;
therefore, this passage deeply clarifies the benefit of the mutual resonance between the Buddha’s response and the practitioner’s invocation.
Next, to reveal the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) of the Sūtra: the selection of the dharma-gate of perfect penetration is like a state selecting its generals for war.
Some are promoted to lead as vanguard; others are pressed into the rear guard. The latter is the true selection;
the others merely follow their respective regular units. These promotions and pressings do not occur without cause. It is just as with the eighteen...

Within the realms (*dhātu*), the standard order is invariably that the sense organs (*indriya*) come first, followed by the objects (*viṣaya*), and finally consciousness (*vijñāna*). Now, however, the six objects are placed first and the organs second.
Among the six objects, the sequence normally begins with form (*rūpa*), followed by sound (*śabda*), and so on through odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharma*).
Here, sound is placed at the very beginning and form follows it. Furthermore, among the six sense organs, only five are listed here; the ear organ (*śrotrendriya*) has been extracted and set aside.

Following the twenty-four gates, it is because the essence of the True Teaching of this land resides in the purity of sound and hearing that he prioritizes the sensory object of sound and places the faculty of hearing last, treating them alone with detailed clarity.
Although he does not explicitly state the reason for this, people have already perceived it.
Having thus placed primary emphasis on the gate of the ear, the essential purport of the entire scripture is arranged as the Dharma-response of Perfect Penetration.

It is so. Nevertheless, the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recollection (*buddhānusmṛti*) is also suited to the capacities of those in this region; sentient beings in the final age must attain deliverance by relying on Buddha-recollection.

Thus, this sutra causes one to enter deeply through a single gate and directly realize one's own nature. If one were to select both gates simultaneously, one would obscure the essential intent of this sutra.
If one were to allow the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recollection to be practiced indiscriminately alongside the common ranks [of other practices], it would likewise fail to fulfill its purpose.
Furthermore, this misses the intent of the extensive praise found in other sutras. Therefore, it now skillfully demonstrates a hidden suppression.
Just as a secret military order is not permitted to be leaked, previously, within the eighteen *dhātus*, the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) was clearly set forth as the primary general;

now, within the seven elements (*mahābhūta*), the element of the faculties (*indriya-mahābhūta*) is implicitly suppressed as the primary general—and this element of the faculties precisely belongs to the Buddha-remembrance practice (*nien-fo*).
This interpretation does not contradict the intent of other sutras that extensively praise [the elements], nor does it deviate from the meaning of this sutra’s use of the sense organs;
it may be called both supremely skillful and supremely subtle. As for the sequence of the seven elements, they are: earth, water, fire, wind, space, seeing, and consciousness.

Seeing is the fundamental faculty; logically, the faculty should come first and consciousness second. Now, consciousness has been moved to the sixth position, while the faculty is placed at the end as the "Great Hall.
This is also like the ear-faculty among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*).

Furthermore, within the preceding five great elements, fire is promoted to the vanguard, with earth, water, wind, and space following in sequence. This has two intentions: first, to accord with the specific needs of the audience.
Because the teaching was initiated by falling into lust, one summons fire through excessive lust to warn those of great learning to first eliminate the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
Therefore, the text says: "It is said that a person of much lust becomes a mass of fierce fire," and so on, up to "transforming the mind of much lust into the fire of wisdom."
The Buddhas called me by the name Huotou (Fire-Head). By the power of the *Agni-prabhā-samādhi*, I have attained Arhatship.
I vow to serve as a powerful warrior to personally subdue the demonic enemies and others, clearly warning them with this light.
In all sūtras and vinayas, non-killing is universally regarded as the foremost precept; however, in this sūtra, celibacy is established as the first and definitive clear instruction. Regarding this—
Among the three conditions, desire and greed likewise precede killing and stealing; this is the intended meaning. Second, it serves as an antidote for the heavy obstacles of the末法 (mofa) age.
Although afflictions are many, sexual desire alone is the root of birth and death, and is most capable of obstructing rebirth in the Dharma.
Therefore, it causes the practitioner to contemplate that the fire of lust within the body of an ordinary person is, in its very nature, the Tathāgatagarbha, which is empty and true.
Fire manifests according to one's karma; through profound contemplation, it is realized and becomes the light of wisdom.
It does not merely fail to obstruct rebirth, but can actually escort the practitioner to be entrusted to the highest grade of rebirth.

Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* praises lust, anger, and ignorance, because their essence is identical to the *tathāgatagarbha*, and the shift between defilement and purity occurs with the turn of a hand. For this reason, the Fire-Head [Avalokiteśvara] is placed first. Furthermore—
They are like Dignāga among the eighteen realms. Now, let us examine the various sages:
apart from these two vanguards and the two heavy generals, all others follow the established precedent exactly, their sequence clearly visible without confusion.

When the twenty-five sages rose from their seats and when the great disciples performed the compilation, their singular majesty and decorum, their single movement and stillness, remained consistent throughout.
All of these possess profound meaning and are entirely in accord with the principles of the teachings. How could one possibly grasp them with a coarse mind?

Nevertheless, although Avalokiteśvara alone has "ascended the examination," how could Śrīkṣetra have failed the exam altogether? It is simply that he is explicitly selected in the case of Avalokiteśvara, whereas he is implicitly selected in the case of Śrīkṣetra.
This is truly because [Avalokiteśvara] enters through a distinct, perfect faculty, while [Śrīkṣetra] encompasses all faculties in their totality.
"Selection by Manifestation": Because this is the teaching-body (*śāstrakāya*) of this region, it is "manifest selection. Because there is a karmic affinity for this land, it is "hidden selection.

It is "manifest selection" because it benefits the immediate practitioners by encompassing sentient beings of the present and future. It is "hidden selection" because it specifically benefits those in the degenerate age of the Dharma who do not see the Buddha.
When one is on the tiger-bannered high list, everyone knows it; when one is secretly marked with a vermilion robe, no one knows.

"Because they do not realize it," [the Master] said. "There is great confusion and error here; one must read and understand it well. Someone asked, "If this is indeed a hidden meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), how can it be leaked?
He replied, "In the arena of the Buddha-selection at the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the proclamation has already been made for over two thousand years.
If it were not clearly revealed and the secret broken open at this time, what would be the use of it? Another person further asked, "If it is truly as you say, then Mañjuśrī spoke..."

When selecting [the dharmas] according to the verses, how could one not also know the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*)? Why not follow the previous precedent and exclude them all at once? The answer is:
because the various sages each personally declared their own teaching to be the foremost; thus, by means of a skillful device of indirect implication, they subtly revealed the profound mechanism.

If one were to strictly select according to the direct command, following the previous track exactly, how could it constitute a "profound" [teaching]? Nevertheless, the element of sound (*śabda*), the object-field of sound (*śabdaviṣaya*), and the fire-element (*tejodhātu*) are, by standard, subsumed under the permanent [category].
Next, these two gates are presented as auxiliary means to clarify specific points; they are not the primary focus of this work, and therefore will not be further elaborated upon.

As for the section on the Dharma-gate of Śrī-Prabhāpāla (Śrī-Ābhāsvara), it follows the prose narrative by being placed after the element of consciousness, serving as the final chapter of the twenty-four gates.
There has never been one who did not follow this principle. Furthermore, since you have already ordered that one specific lineage be selected, how could you fail to choose Śrīmatī?
Observe her words of selection; they still differ from those of the other sages. She simply says: "The causes and effects are now distinct; how can one attain perfect penetration?"

The meaning is this: although those [practitioners] have fully integrated the six sense faculties and their pure mindfulness continues in succession, this successive mindfulness—being part of the flux of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations)—is itself a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing.
To take this as a cause while desiring to be reborn to see the Buddha—who could say it is impossible?

However, if one now wishes to realize the non-arising and non-ceasing perfect penetration (*pariśuddhi*) through direct evidence, then cause and effect do not correspond; how then could such a goal be achieved? This...
The selection [of Avalokiteśvara] is based on attaining perfect penetration in the present life; it does not concern the benefits obtained after rebirth.

As for the other sages, who contemplate their own individual buddha-natures, these belong solely to present cultivation and present realization. Therefore, they are entirely excluded, as they do not accord with the spiritual capacities of the beings in this land.

This is because it does not accord with the essential substance of this teaching. Those who are determined to cultivate and realize [the truth] should also reflect upon this deeply and for a long time.

However, this is spoken for those whose power of faith is not yet firm. If one possesses deep faith in the Pure Land, even if the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* were to single out and disparage Śrī-Ābhāsvara (Potisai), one would still harbor no doubt. Why is this? Because other sutras praise him extensively. Thus, it is said: "It is inconceivable."

When discussing its merits, it is called "a teaching difficult for the world to believe," "that which is protected by all Buddhas," "the unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous dhyāna," "the supreme and extraordinary skillful means," and "the king among samādhis. Though praised extensively in many places, people still fail to give rise to faith.

If it were merely disparaged in one place, why would you suddenly give rise to doubt? Moreover, it was never disparaged in isolation; furthermore, it was even shown to have been chosen through an "obscure" selection.

Alas, sentient beings of the末法 (final dharma) age who read this sutra are unable to follow the teachings to enter deeply through the gateway of the ear and realize perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) through direct manifestation.
Instead, they harbor suspicions particularly regarding the Buddha-remembrance (*nianfo*) dharma-gate, even going so far as to destroy the pure faith of others.
This obstructs the virtuous conduct of others; such is the habitual tendency of those with meager merit and little wisdom.
Therefore, I have here analyzed the matter in detail according to the Dharma and based upon the sūtras, though I am unaware that my words have become so prolix. How could I help it?

Regarding the three characters for "traveling" (*lǚ*), the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The three realms offer no peace; they are like a burning house. If one is greedily attached and gives rise to craving, one will be consumed by fire.
Therefore, the World-Honored One, the Buddha of the past, used skillful means to exhort and advise, leading them out from within this dwelling. Thus, the multitude within this dwelling...
Suffering is pervasive; it is difficult to dwell in peace. As the Great Master Ouyi states in his *Collection on Pure Faith*:

"From the true nature of the *sambhogakāya* (寂光) downward, one is obscured by the defilements of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*). Consequently, among all sentient beings, few ever abide permanently.

Even the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and the land of expedient means (*upāyabhūmi*) are merely places of temporary lodging. How great is the significance of the concept of 'lodging'! For those who travel..."
A traveler is one who stays at an inn; such a traveler must have companions, must have a place to stay, and must have their own primary occupation.
Now, when we look broadly across the three realms, they are all like travelers on the same journey. Yet, people differ in their occupations;
since their primary occupations differ, their places and companions likewise diverge. Alas, since the dawn of consciousness, we have passed through dust-like aeons...
Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the bones one has accumulated exceed Mount Sumeru, and the milk one has drunk surpasses the vastness of the oceans.
Within this time, the state of wandering in misery and the suffering of drifting in uncertainty are beyond description; yet at such times, one is a companion to those of the hells.
This is because malice and rebellion are its root, and the *sāntara* and *avīci* hells are its dwelling places. At such times, one is a companion to those of the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
When stinginess and greed are its basis, the wilderness, mountains, and marshes are its dwelling place, and it takes the animal realm as its companions.
When ignorance is its basis, the realms of water, land, and air are its dwelling place, and it takes the asuras as its companions.
When anger and pride are its basis, Mount Sumeru and the great ocean are its dwelling place.

When one is a companion to the human realm, the fundamental principles of social order (*gangchang*) constitute its basis; the various nations of the four continents are its temporary dwelling places.
When one is a companion to the desire heavens (*kāmadhātu*), the precepts and wholesome deeds constitute its basis; the earth-dwelling and space-dwelling deities are its temporary dwelling places.
When one is a companion to the form and formless realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) constitutes its basis; the four dhyānas [are its dwelling places].
The four emptinesses are one’s temporary lodgings. While staying in these lodgings, one becomes attached to each place and fails to realize that they are merely temporary. Alas!
Even the dreams of one’s native land remain hazy; how could dwelling in a guest-house ever be the ultimate destination?

If one does not entrust oneself to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) to transcend horizontally, and awaken to the Land of Quiescent Light (Ji-guang) to penetrate upward, who then could escape the meaning of being a traveler?
The lay practitioner Wang Runcheng of Tiandu, whose Dharma name is Xingjing and pen-name Lüsan, has been away from home traveling and studying for many years.
In his later years, he resided in Qinchuan, where he had a filial son who was preeminent in talent and had long managed the family estate;

thus, the lay practitioner was not burdened by domestic affairs. Although he possessed grand buildings and magnificent halls in which to enjoy his retirement, to the lay practitioner’s eyes, these appeared utterly desolate.

If he were merely a guest, this layman would have long been engaged in the practice of fasting and serving the Buddha; he would have cultivated himself through detachment and freedom from desire, and would have remained ever vigilant in his moral discipline and pursuit of the Way.
On the first day of the second month of autumn in the year of Kāngxī Yimao (1695), it was the anniversary of his seventieth birthday.
His many relatives, friends, and old acquaintances vied with one another to compose writings to congratulate him and poems to praise him. The layman declined them and did not look at them;
even when he did look, he did so without close attention, saying: "These are merely distractions for the ears and eyes.

Rather than the arrival of flattering words to purchase my reputation, how much better it would be for the arrival of Dharma words to benefit my mind. Thus, he took the characters from the hexagram *Liu-san* (The Third Line of the Sixth Hexagram) and...
Please speak to me. I reflect that you, householder, have already journeyed through the three realms; you are truly one who has attained the greatness of travel.
How could it be merely a matter of the capital cities or the market towns?

Yet, as I observe the people and officials of your state, many of them engage in speculative trade and travel in all directions. In their travels, they seek only to secure profit, yet they do not exhaust its full potential.
This is indeed the meaning. Now you, Layman, are traveling here. Suppose there were someone who informed you of a scheme to profit from boiling the sea, or presented to you the strategy of Mr.
Guo for governing a mountain; I know that you would surely cover your ears and depart from such things.
Yet, on this occasion of your seventieth birthday, you alone have been able to decline the wine of your friends without a second thought and set aside the sacrificial cauldrons.

Yet he does not indulge in worldly affairs; instead, he seeks me out on the shores of withered desolation and profound stillness, consulting me on the principles of transcending the age and departing from convention.
One might say that his true purity has not yet dissipated and the great simplicity still remains—is he not one who is close to the Way? I reply: "Not yet.
For once it is said that 'traveling' is threefold, then all dharmas tend toward traveling; there is no dharma whatsoever that exceeds traveling."
This refers to being attached to whatever place one happens upon, not realizing that it is merely a temporary lodging. One understands that these three realms are all alike a transient inn;

that the objects of one's past karma are but fellow travelers, each distinct from the other, and are merely "lodgers" by name. Knowing they are not one's home, one does not dwell in them nor become attached to them.
Not giving rise to craving or attachment toward coarse and inferior objects is the practice of observing the journey. Regarding adventitious afflictions, [one employs] skillful means...

Subduing [the afflictions], the long journey of the dream-like state is as if about to awaken; it is like being a traveler, yet not departing from the Dharma-realm while dwelling within the mundane world.
Compassionately aiding these travelers, one provides full assistance across the ferry; this is the realization of the traveler. This dilapidated old house belongs to a single person;
I have always been here preaching the Dharma and transforming beings. Even when the great fire burns, my land remains peaceful and secure.
This is the ultimate journey. If one does not comprehend this meaning, then one will mistakenly take the waystations and lodgings for one’s true home;

all that one seeks will be nothing but affairs within the burning house. Furthermore, if out of fear of the hardships and sufferings of this journey, one turns the mind toward [the final destination] with such urgency as to depart without ever returning, then the six realms will be plunged into universal darkness. Upon whom can the four modes of birth rely in such a state?

None of these truly accord with the meaning of being a traveler. Therefore, for a *gṛhapati* (lay practitioner) in the present day, one should take the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*) as one’s final destination;
do not remain forever a transient guest in this world of endurance (*saṃsāra*).

Furthermore, when the lotus blooms and you behold the Buddha, attaining realization of the true and eternal, you should look back upon this Sahā world and return once more to reside here as a sojourner, protecting your fellow companions and guiding the multitudes.
I am deluded. Yet, you manifest your body and trace your presence in various distant lands and foreign regions, coming and going through the three realms without ever growing weary;
you are truly an ultimate traveler, perhaps not in vain bearing the meaning of the title "Layman" (Upāsaka).

Regarding the method for contemplating the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the hair-treasure) of the Buddha, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "Those who wish to be born in the Western Land should contemplate the image one zhang and six chi in height upon the surface of the water.
It further states: "The bodily marks and signs are so numerous that they cannot be contemplated all at once; one must enter through a single mark or sign. That is to say:
Focus exclusively on the single mark of the white tuft (ūrṇā-kośa). Wait until this visualization is matured; then the other marks will manifest spontaneously.
The tuft is one zhang and five chi in length, with a circumference of five cun. It has eight facets on the outside, while the interior is hollow and translucent, resembling a tube of lapis lazuli.
Between the two eyebrows, it represents the Middle Way. It spirals to the right, as white as jade or snow, pure, brilliant, and translucent, shining upon the golden body.
When visualizing in this manner, cause the mind to remain firmly established. If the mind becomes dull or distracted, restrain it to make it clear and still.
For clarity prevents dullness and stillness prevents distraction; one should know that clarity and stillness are the effects of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. This is concentration (*samādhi*).
The essence of wisdom (*prajñā*) is also the fundamental substance of the mind. Calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are the methods of practice;

concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom are the causal practices; clarity and stillness are the functional effects. When clarity and stillness reach their ultimate limit, one suddenly accords with the fundamental substance.

Upon reaching the fruition, this becomes the two kinds of adornment: merit and wisdom. Now, the body and mind are tranquil and settled—this is calm abiding. Contemplating the Buddha’s *ūrṇā-kośa* (the hair-treasure between the eyebrows)—this is insight. As for the hair-treasure...

"Li" (歷然) means clarity. "Ming" (明) means being firmly established and unmoving; this is stillness (*śamatha*). What is meant is that by relying upon those physical forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), one perfumes one's own mind-nature (*citta-dharmatā*);

once contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) is perfected, [the truth] manifests spontaneously. This is precisely the meaning of this principle. However, if one wishes to cultivate this contemplation, one must understand that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are mind-only (*cittamātra*).
As the Sūtra says: "The mind is like a skilled painter, creating the various five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); within all worlds..."
There is nothing that is not created from the mind. Therefore, one should know that the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) of Amitābha is inherently possessed by my own mind;

its manifestation within meditative concentration is likewise produced by my own mind. This mind creates the tuft of hair, and this mind is the tuft of hair. It is not obtained from another, nor does it come from without.
To realize and penetrate this is what is called practicing contemplation in accordance with the Dharma. In short, it is the capacity for contemplation.
The contemplating wisdom constitutes the three contemplations within a single mind; the object contemplated—the mark of the ūrṇā-kośa—is the three truths within a single realm.

Why is this so? Although the mark of the ūrṇā-kośa appears before one in meditative concentration, it is entirely produced through the conditions of mental recollection and lacks any real nature or characteristic.
These phenomena born of causes and conditions are, by their very nature (dharmatā), devoid of self-nature, other-nature, common nature, and causeless nature—thus they lack these four natures.

All are empty; therefore, they lack substantial nature. Furthermore, the tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) produced by this conceptualization is not only empty in nature, but its marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are also utterly unobtainable—like a reflection in a mirror or the moon in water—and thus it lacks substantial marks.
Since both nature and marks lack substance, it is emptiness and the ultimate (*paramārtha*).

Because one can see it according to thought, it is the provisional and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Because it is the provisional and the conventional, it is not true emptiness; it is precisely emptiness.
It is precisely the ultimate truth; therefore, it is not a conventional fiction. This constitutes a single thought-moment in which negation and illumination occur simultaneously.

It is beyond both identity and difference, yet it is both identical and non-identical. Thus, it is the contemplative object of the Middle Way, wherein the three and the one are perfectly interfused and inconceivable.

The truth gives rise to contemplation, and contemplation in turn illuminates the truth; object and contemplation are non-dual, being nothing other than the One Mind. As an ancient master’s verse says:
The object is wondrously provisional; the contemplation is empty. The simultaneous vanishing of both object and contemplation is the Middle Way.

How could cessation and illumination ever have a sequence? Within the single mind, all is fused and severed, leaving no trace at all. This verse is concise and elliptical; its meaning must be briefly explained.

To say that the object is "wondrously provisional" implies that emptiness and the Middle Way are already contained therein. Without possessing both emptiness and the Middle Way, how could it be called "wondrously provisional"? As for the contemplation...
To speak of emptiness is to mean wondrous emptiness; therein, the Middle and the Provisional are already contained.

To say that both object and contemplation are simultaneously extinguished implies that simultaneous illumination is already contained therein. Simultaneous extinction means neither empty nor provisional; simultaneous illumination means both empty and provisional.
Not adhering to the two extremes, yet not departing from them either, it is therefore the Middle Way. The following two phrases state that forgetting and illumination are simultaneous;

the one mind is thus fused and transcendent. Although the objects of contemplation comprise three aspects, as they belong to the objective realm being observed, they are simply termed "wondrous conventionality.

Although the modes of contemplation comprise three aspects, as they belong to the subjective contemplation observing them, they are simply named "wondrous emptiness. Although the object and the contemplation...

Each possesses the three. Having employed the wondrous contemplation that simultaneously negates and illuminates both, one darkly accords with the wondrous realm that simultaneously transcends and affirms both.
This is simply within the marvelous; thus, by taking up one, all three are present, and speaking of the three, they are one. One and three are not the same; the three and the three are not different.
It cannot be deliberated upon by the conscious intellect, nor can it be distinguished by names and words; therefore, it is said to be "lost" (wáng).
Illumination—how could it ever have before or after? With the single mind fused and severed, there is no trace at all.

This wondrous principle of the perfect fusion of object and contemplation is fully encompassed by these four lines without omission. This marvelous gāthā is superior to reading several hundred scrolls of the Tiantai school’s texts.
However, for those who have not clearly realized the One Mind and have not yet mastered the Tiantai teachings, it is feared that this will not be easily penetrated. A sutra states:

"Merely hearing the name of the White Tuft [of hair] extinguishes immeasurable sins; how much more so when one contemplates according to the Dharma what was revealed from the golden mouth of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
The Tiantai Master Zhiyi exhorted others to practice this exclusively. In recent times, only the Great Master Youxi has constantly cultivated it.
Contemplation: Now, if practitioners of pure karma can single-mindedly hold the Name, rebirth [in the Pure Land] may be assured;
if they further cultivate the wondrous contemplations, their station upon arrival will surely be high. Why, then, do those of sharp faculties and superior caliber not strive to practice this?
Admonition (End)
